Learning Objectives
Describe the epidemiology, etiology, evaluation, and diagnosis of knee osteoarthritis.
Determine the role of nonsurgical management of knee osteoarthritis.
Assess common nonarthroplasty surgical treatment options for patients with knee
osteoarthritis.

Osteoarthritis is the leading cause of disability and impaired quality of life in developed
countries in patients older than 65 years.
As the population ages, the prevalence of osteoarthritis is expected to increase 66% to 100%
by 2030.
Osteoarthritis affects all ethnic groups and geographic locations.
It is more common in women than men.
The knee is the most commonly affected joint, with 12% of adults older than 60 years
diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis.
Risk factors
Advancing age (perhaps the most important risk factor)
Female sex: loss of estrogen over time increases risk
Genetics
Obesity

Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis
The disease process usually involves all of the tissues that form the synovial joint,
including the articular cartilage, subchondral bone, metaphyseal bone, synovium,
ligaments, joint capsule, and muscles crossing the joint.
The etiology of osteoarthritis is multifactorial. On a cellular level, osteoarthritis appears
to be the result of deterioration in the ability of chondrocytes to maintain and restore
articular cartilage. Evidence shows that chondrocytes undergo age-related telomere
erosion, and increased expression of the senescence marker, ß-galactosidase, suggests
that cell senescence is responsible for the age-related loss of chondrocyte function.
Overall, women are disproportionately affected at a higher rate than men; men younger
than 55 years are diagnosed at a higher rate than women.
Evaluation of the Knee
Patient History
Pain often is exacerbated with activity and relieved by rest.

Some degree of deformity
Patellar tracking and ligament stability should be assessed.
Varus or valgus alignment should be noted.
Any gait abnormality
Patients with osteoarthritis have an altered gait and increased energy cost.
Atrophy in muscles crossing the affected joint often is present in patients with chronic disease.
Radiography
Weight-bearing radiographs are the most sensitive for confirming the diagnosis of
osteoarthritis.
PA views in 45° of flexion (Rosenberg view) and sunrise views may demonstrate osteoarthritis
not visible on standard AP and lateral views.
Full-length standing views are used to evaluate the mechanical axis of the lower limb (Figure
1).
Radiographic changes
Narrowing of the cartilage space
Increased density of the subchondral bone (sclerosis)
Osteophytes
In more severe cases:
Subchondral cysts (geodes)
Loose bodies
Joint subluxation
Deformity
Malalignment may be present.

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management of knee osteoarthritis is focused on symptomatic relief; however, it
may not alter the natural course of the disease.
According to the most recent Osteoarthritis Research Society International guidelines:
Arthritis education and structured land-based exercise programs with or without dietary
weight management are the core recommended nonsurgical treatment options for knee
osteoarthritis.2
Management based on the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-Based
Clinical Practice Guideline on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee
Strong recommendations for patients with symptomatic osteoarthritis of the knee:
Self-management programs, strengthening, low-impact aerobic exercises, and
neuromuscular education; and engaging in physical activity consistent with national
guidelines.
NSAIDs (oral or topical)
Cannot recommend oral narcotic agents because they result in a considerable increase in
adverse events and are not effective treatment options.
Tramadol previously was recommended as a second-line treatment option for knee
osteoarthritis in patients in whom NSAIDs failed to provide adequate pain relief.
Cannot recommend using acupuncture
Cannot recommend using glucosamine and chondroitin.
Cannot recommend using hyaluronic acid.
Moderate recommendations
Weight loss for patients with symptomatic osteoarthritis of the knee and a body mass index
(BMI) greater or equal to 25 kg/m2
Cannot suggest that lateral wedge insoles be used for patients with symptomatic medial
compartment osteoarthritis of the knee


Nonsurgical Management
The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-Based Clinical Practice
Guideline on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee provides important evidenced-
based recommendations for the management of patients with symptomatic knee
osteoarthritis. Nonsurgical management typically involves a multimodal strategy to
control a patient’s symptoms. This often begins with arthritis education and a structured
exercise program and/or formal physical therapy, with or without dietary weight
management for patients with an elevated BMI. Anti-inflammatory medications, such as
oral or topical NSAIDs, can be added to the treatment regimen. In patients in whom
these treatment options fail and patients with severe debilitating pain, corticosteroid
injection may be offered to help reduce pain, swelling, and stiffness in the knee and
better allow patients to participate in physical activities. In patients with
unicompartmental osteoarthritis, the use of an unloader brace also may be attempted.
Although evidence against the use of glucosamine, chondroitin, and intra-articular
hyaluronic acid injections exists, some patients experience relief from these
medications, and patients can be counseled regarding these treatment options.
Research to evaluate the effectiveness of intra-articular platelet-rich plasma in patients
with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis is ongoing. In patients in whom nonsurgical

Nonarthroplasty Surgical Treatment Options
Introduction
Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is a proven treatment option for end-stage knee osteoarthritis.
However, in younger patients with pain and functional limitations because of knee
osteoarthritis or those who do not wish to proceed with TKA, knee joint preservation has
increased in popularity with advances in surgical techniques.
Knee Arthroscopy With Débridement or Partial Meniscectomy
In younger patients with primarily mechanical symptoms who have a meniscal tear and mild
osteoarthritis, arthroscopic surgery may be indicated if nonsurgical treatment options fail.
In patients with moderate to severe osteoarthritis or more than 50% joint space loss,
arthroscopy generally is not recommended.
The addition of microfracture or abrasion chondroplasty to penetrate the subchondral bone
and stimulate the growth of fibrocartilage also has shown to result in no added benefit in
patients with knee osteoarthritis.

Knee Arthroscopy With Débridement or Partial Meniscectomy
The Meniscal Repair in Osteoarthritis Research trial was a multicenter, randomized,
controlled trial of patients 45 years or older with a symptomatic meniscal tear and mild-
to-moderate osteoarthritis who were randomly assigned to a standardized physical
therapy program or arthroscopic partial meniscectomy and postoperative physical
therapy. Both groups had substantial improvements in functional outcomes, but the
outcomes did not differ substantially at 6 and 12 months. However, 30% of patients in
the physical therapy group crossed over to surgical treatment within 6 months.3 This
emphasizes the importance of exhausting nonsurgical treatment options, including
physical therapy, in patients with a degenerative meniscal tear. In patients who remain
symptomatic, arthroscopic surgery may be considered.

Arthroscopic lavage and débridement for primarily knee osteoarthritis is not supported
in the literature. A randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial by Moseley et al4 found
no differences between groups that underwent arthroscopic lavage and débridement
versus a sham surgery (placebo) over 24 months. Thorlund et al5 performed a systematic
review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials assessing the benefit of
arthroscopic surgery involving partial meniscectomy, débridement, or both for patients
with and without radiographic signs of osteoarthritis. Although arthroscopy was
associated with some early benefit with regard to pain at 3 and 6 months, this benefit
was absent 1 to 2 years postoperatively. In addition, no added benefit for physical
function was observed, and complications are associated with surgical management,
including infection, deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and death.
Realignment Osteotomy for Unicompartmental Osteoarthritis Associated With Varus or Valgus
Malalignment
Valgus-producing osteotomy for medial compartment osteoarthritis
In patients with isolated medial compartment osteoarthritis, valgus-producing osteotomies
are a well-proven surgical treatment option.
Medial opening wedge high tibial osteotomy (HTO) is commonly used to manage medial knee
osteoarthritis in patients with varus malalignment (Figure 2).

Varus-producing osteotomy for lateral compartment osteoarthritis
Distal femur osteotomy (DFO) typically is performed to correct valgus deformity associated
with lateral compartment osteoarthritis (Figure 3).
The goal is to relieve lateral compartment pain and slow the progression of osteoarthritis by
shifting the mechanical axis into neutral or slight varus, which can be achieved via lateral
opening wedge or medial closing wedge DFO.


Realignment Osteotomy for Unicompartmental Osteoarthritis
Associated With Varus or Valgus Malalignment
As unicompartmental knee osteoarthritis progresses, deformity secondary to loss of the
joint space may develop within the affected compartment. As joint space narrowing
progresses, this may lead to knee varus if the medial compartment is affected or valgus
if the lateral compartment is affected. This may contribute to worsening symptoms as
the mechanical axis shifts further into the medial or lateral compartment, respectively. In
addition, patients with constitutional varus or valgus may develop unicompartmental
osteoarthritis and be at risk for rapid progression because of medial or lateral
compartment overload. By offloading the arthritic compartment, realignment osteotomy
of the proximal tibia or the distal femur may improve symptoms and function.
The goal is to relieve medial compartment pain and slow the progression of
osteoarthritis by shifting the mechanical axis into neutral or slight valgus, which can be
achieved via a medial opening wedge or lateral closing wedge HTO. The ideal surgical
candidate is a younger patient (<60 years) with isolated medial arthritis, preserved knee
range of motion, and a ligamentously stable knee.6,7 Often, a trial with a medial
unloader brace can be used to determine suitability; if the patient has a good response
with the use of the unloader brace, this is a positive predictive factor for successful HTO.
Good clinical outcomes are reported with concomitant HTO and ACL reconstruction. In
older patients, this can be performed in a staged fashion with an initial HTO, and if
patients remain symptomatic, ACL reconstruction can be performed during a second-
stage surgical procedure.8
Additional consideration should be given to the posterior tibial slope in an ACL-deficient
knee. Elevated posterior tibial slope is a risk factor for ACL injury and ACL graft
failure.9,10 In performing HTO in an ACL-deficient knee, a slope-reducing technique
should be used for optimal results11 (Figure 4).

If HTO is performed in combination with osteochondral allografting or autologous
chondrocyte implantation, the goal is to create a biomechanically favorable environment
for biologic healing. A recent study demonstrated that a neutral mechanical axis

provided the most ideal mechanical environment for osteochondral allografting and
autologous chondrocyte implantation in their cohort for survivorship.12
The results of HTO vary within the literature, and wide heterogeneity exists among
studies. In general, HTO affords good relief of pain and restores function for medial knee
osteoarthritis.6,13 Survivorship of medial opening wedge and lateral closing wedge HTO
has been reported range from 70% to 94% at 5 to 9 years, 74% to 98% at 10 years, 66%
to 91% at 15 years, and 52% to 54% at 17 or 18 years. Poor prognostic factors with HTO
include severe medial osteoarthritis, advanced age, patellofemoral arthritis, decreased
range of motion, joint instability, and lateral tibial thrust.6,7
The results of HTO versus UKA are similar, with studies reporting HTO to be superior for
returning to full activities, such as running or sports, in younger patients14and other
studies reporting UKA to result in better functional outcomes.15 Revision to TKA is largely
equivocal with modern HTO and UKA techniques, with both posing unique challenges;
however, UKA has demonstrated a lower conversion rate to TKA.15 Overall, HTO and
UKA are viable treatment options to delay TKA, with HTO being preferable in younger,
more active patients who desire to maintain a higher level of activity without concern for
accelerated wear of the arthroplasty components or early loosening.7
In the largest series on lateral opening wedge DFO, Cameron et al18 reported on 30
patients (31 knees) at a mean follow-up of 5 years (range, 2 to 12 years). The authors
reported considerable improvement in International Knee Documentation Committee
scores, with 74% free of arthroplasty in the arthritis group (19 knees with a mean age of
41 years) and 92% free of arthroplasty in the joint preservation group (12 knees with a
mean age of 26 years). In a recent systematic review of 14 studies, including 236 patients
who underwent closing wedge DFO and 71 patients who underwent opening wedge DFO
with a mean age of 49 years, Chahla et al19 reported good to excellent patient-reported
outcomes, with a mean survival rate of 80% at a follow-up of 10 years. DFO may be
considered a viable treatment option for delaying TKA and may improve pain and
function in patients with valgus deformity and lateral compartment arthritis; however,
results are expected to deteriorate over time.

Pearls and Pitfalls
Knee osteoarthritis is a leading cause of disability and impaired quality of life, and in younger,
active patients, alternatives to knee arthroplasty are valuable treatment considerations.
Full-length standing radiographs are important in the evaluation of patients with knee
osteoarthritis to determine the mechanical axis of the lower limb and if any varus or valgus
malalignment is present.
Nonsurgical treatment recommendations include activity modifications, self-directed exercise
programs, physical therapy, weight loss, and NSAIDs.
Inconclusive evidence for or against the use of unloader bracing, intra-articular steroids, and
manual therapy exists according to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-
Based Clinical Practice Guideline on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee.
In younger patients with mild osteoarthritis only and a symptomatic meniscus tear refractory
to nonsurgical management, arthroscopic partial meniscectomy may be considered.
In older patients and in patients with moderate to severe osteoarthritis, arthroscopy is not
recommended.
The ideal surgical candidate for HTO is a younger, more active patient with isolated medial
arthritis, varus malalignment, preserved knee range of motion, and a stable knee.
DFO is a viable treatment option for delaying TKA and may improve pain and function in
patients with valgus deformity and isolated lateral compartment arthritis.
